As a result of the proximity of these vegetation types to meandering creeks and drainages distinct patterns, frequently contrasting with flatter surrounding grasslands, often emerge. Ponderosa pine is a visually dominant vegetation type within the tracts. More densely forested areas generally follow drainages, ridges, and are scattered along hilltops, forming visual features and patterns contrasting in texture, and color and enclosure with the grasslands and shrubs. Grasslands provide a generally homogeneous, smooth textured vegetation cover. Color variations are subtle ranging in hues from light yellow to greens or tans, depending upon the time of year and dominant grass species. Perceptually, one of the most dominant features of the grasslands is the open view of the surrounding landscape that exists where topography permits.
Scattered fields of dry cropland are located predominantly on the upper plateau areas of Tracts II and III, and within the bottom lands of Sarpy Creek and the east fork of Sarpy Creek. Depending upon the time of year, these fields, used primarily for the cultivation of alfalfa and small grains, create distinctly shaped areas differing in texture and color with the surrounding grasslands, shrubs and trees.
The aesthetic interest of the Sarpy Creek Basin is in part related to some of the old buildings still remaining in the area. Of twenty-three structures or groups of structures located within Tracts II and III, one is considered negative, 15 are considered neutral, and seven are considered to be positive scenic influences (Westmoreland Resources, 1975 g). In general, most of the buildings which may be considered to be of positive scenic interest are old homesteads, ranches and barns constructed of wood or log materials.
